last_attempts_log.asr_text: You go to buy your usual coffee, but then you stop. Hey, when did you become so fancy? Tariffs are the first thing you think of. You want to say, so you're to blame. But a good detective stops and thinks first. Let's turn back the clock and examine this case. Reports based on government figures say the average U.S. price of ground coffee rose 41 percent. That was compared with the same month a year earlier. This is about ground coffee, not a cup in a café. Before coffee wakes you up, its price shocks your wallet awake. But Reuters says most of the rise in store prices came from bean shortages and higher bean prices. Those shortages began before the summer tariffs. Wait a minute, our case began before the suspect we watched even appeared.

last_attempts_log.asr_text: The investigation leads us to Brazil. A drought was happening there. People had also stopped hoping that the next harvest would be better. Will there be enough beans? Before we think about how to brew them, we must ask if there will be any beans to brew at all. We turn the pages of the record and find this: in February, before summer, New York's Arabica coffee futures price reached a record high. This was not the price of ground coffee in stores, it was the market price for trading coffee beans. The market alarm had already sounded. So were tariffs not to blame? No, that would be deciding too soon, too. Reuters also reported that U.S. tariffs put in place during summer raised the price of the beans themselves. They did play a part. But we must put events in the right order.

last_attempts_log.asr_text: Here is a key point: At the time of that report, the tariff-caused rise had not yet passed through the whole supply chain. It had not fully reached the prices shoppers paid. When bean costs rise, the store price tag does not jump up at once and say, got it. Price rises take time to appear. In other words, a price tag is not live news. It is like a letter that arrives a little late. You may open it today, but it may not be about something that happened today. It may tell you about an earlier drought, a bean shortage, or high market prices. If you look only at the latest headline, you may name the wrong sender. Next time, take a second look at a store price tag. Ask, why is it expensive? Then add, when did this happen? Coffee may taste bitter, but we want our detective work to be clear. Before that first cup, turn the clock back a little.
